bullets: ‘Is this a dagger which I see before me, / The handle toward my hand? Come, let me clutch thee.’: **rhetorical question** shows uncertainty; the handle offered towards him suggests temptation.
‘A dagger of the mind, a false creation, / Proceeding from the heat-oppressed brain?’: he wonders whether it is a **hallucination**: guilt and fever, or the supernatural?
‘And on thy blade and dudgeon gouts of blood’: the vision becomes bloody, **foreshadowing** the murder.
‘Now o’er the one half-world / Nature seems dead’: darkness, witchcraft (‘Hecate’) and ‘withered murder’ personified creeping like a ghost: **gothic atmosphere**.
‘Hear it not, Duncan, for it is a knell / That summons thee to heaven or to hell.’: **rhyming couplet** closes the scene with a death-bell; decisive.

callouts.p: The dagger is ambiguous: supernatural or psychological. Strong answers discuss both, and link to Banquo’s ghost (3.4).

core.p: Waiting for the bell that signals the time to kill, Macbeth sees a dagger floating before him.

bullets: ‘I have done the deed.’: **euphemism**; he cannot say ‘murder’.
Short, broken lines of dialogue (‘Did not you speak?’ / ‘When?’ / ‘Now.’ / ‘As I descended?’) create **stichomythia**: tension and panic.
‘This is a sorry sight.’: guilt begins at once.
He could not say ‘Amen’: cut off from God’s grace.
‘Methought I heard a voice cry “Sleep no more! / Macbeth does murder sleep”’: **sleep** = innocence and peace; he has destroyed his own rest. Motif returns in 3.2 and 5.1.

‘Will all great Neptune’s ocean wash this blood / Clean from my hand? No, this my hand will rather / The multitudinous seas incarnadine, / Making the green one red.’: **hyperbole**; guilt so vast it could stain the oceans. Contrast of Latinate grandeur (‘multitudinous… incarnadine’) and plain monosyllables (‘Making the green one red’).
Lady Macbeth: ‘Had he not resembled / My father as he slept, I had done’t.’: a crack in her resolve; humanity glimpsed.
‘My hands are of your colour, but I shame / To wear a heart so white.’: she mocks his cowardice.
‘A little water clears us of this deed.’: **dramatic irony**; compare 5.1 ‘Out, damned spot!’
core.p: Macbeth returns with bloody daggers, horrified. Lady Macbeth takes control and returns the daggers to frame the grooms.

bullets: Porter: ‘Knock, knock, knock! Who’s there, i’ th’ name of Beelzebub?’: **comic relief** in prose, but it makes Macbeth’s castle literally **hell**.
‘Here’s an equivocator’: probable reference to the Jesuit Henry Garnet, executed after the **Gunpowder Plot** for equivocation; links to the Witches’ double meanings.
Macduff: ‘O horror, horror, horror!’: **tricolon**; language fails.
‘Most sacrilegious murder hath broke ope / The Lord’s anointed temple’: killing a king is attacking God (**divine right**).
Macbeth’s over-elaborate grief (‘His silver skin laced with his golden blood’) is suspiciously poetic: performance.
Lady Macbeth ‘faints’: genuine or a distraction? Discuss both.
core.h: Act 2 Scene 3: the Porter and the discovery
core.p: Knocking at the gate; the drunken Porter imagines himself the porter of hell. Macduff discovers Duncan’s body. Macbeth kills the grooms. Malcolm and Donalbain flee.

bullets: Day is dark: ‘darkness does the face of earth entomb’.
‘A falcon, towering in her pride of place, / Was by a mousing owl hawked at and killed’: the natural order inverted, like a subject killing a king (**Great Chain of Being**).
Duncan’s horses ‘ate each other’: chaos in nature.
Macbeth has gone to Scone to be crowned; Macduff refuses to attend: first sign of resistance.
core.p: Ross and an Old Man describe unnatural events since the murder.

essays.q: Explore how Shakespeare presents guilt in Act 2 Scene 2.
essays.text: Shakespeare dramatises guilt through the language of the scene’s first lines. Macbeth cannot name his crime, reducing it to the euphemism ‘I have done the deed’, and the stichomythic exchange that follows, ‘Did not you speak?’ / ‘When?’ / ‘Now.’, fractures the iambic pentameter into anxious fragments. His guilt then becomes spiritual: he could not say ‘Amen’, and he hears a voice cry ‘Macbeth does murder sleep’. Sleep, which the play associates with innocence and healing, has been killed alongside Duncan, so Macbeth has punished himself in the act of murder. The scene’s climax is his question, ‘Will all great Neptune’s ocean wash this blood / Clean from my hand?’, answered with the hyperbole that his hand will ‘incarnadine’ the seas. The shift from the grand Latinate ‘multitudinous seas incarnadine’ to the blunt monosyllables of ‘Making the green one red’ shows a mind lurching from enormity to simple horror. Lady Macbeth’s reply, ‘A little water clears us of this deed’, is chillingly practical; but the audience, who will see her washing invisible blood in Act 5, recognises the dramatic irony.
essays.thesis: Shakespeare shows guilt overwhelming Macbeth immediately, while Lady Macbeth’s dismissal of it sets up her later collapse.
why: Close AO2: euphemism, stichomythia, motif, hyperbole, diction contrast, irony.

mistakes.w: The Porter scene is just a joke.

mistakes.w: Lady Macbeth feels no guilt in Act 2.

summary: Act 2 contains the dagger soliloquy (2.1), the murder’s aftermath (2.2), the Porter and the discovery (2.3) and the unnatural omens (2.4): learn the key lines on guilt, blood, sleep, the supernatural and disorder, and how to analyse them in a part (a) answer.
